messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We'll meet at our regular time on Monday, 3-5PM in Wickson 2124.

I'll be giving a short talk on vectorization in R in the first half of the session.  New R users' are often told to vectorize their code, but vectorization does different things in different cases.  I'll do my best to explain how vectorization works internally in R, why it's sometimes helpful in making code faster or less error-prone, and when you should try to vectorize.

Following the talk, we'll have our regular co-working/Q&A/cookie eating time.

Best,

Noam

Joint Statistics – Linguistics Seminar

Thursday, April 10th 2014 at 4:10pm, MSB 1147 (Colloquium Room)

Please join us for refreshments at 3:30pm in MSB 1147 (Colloquium Room)

Speaker:              Stefan Gries

UC Santa Barbara

Title:                      "Quantitative methods in corpus linguistics: examples and requests for feedback”

Abstract:              Corpus linguistics is a linguistic methodology based on the exploration/analysis of (ideally) large amounts of data retrieved from textual databases. Even though this method has been around for several decades and even though it is by definition a quantitative approach, it is only in the last 10 years or so that more and more advanced quantitative methods have become more widespread. As a result, the field is still very much in flux as practitioners are trying to develop suitable methods to deal with the large amounts of often very noisy and interrelated data. In this talk, I will present several problems that corpus linguists have (begun) to deal with in recent work with an eye to (i) giving an overview of current considerations in corpus linguistics and (ii) getting feedback on some suggestions that have been made. The areas/questions I will discuss involve (depending on time):

•             how to quantify the association/repulsion between words in corpora - the roles of directionality and diversity of association;

•             how to quantify the distribution of words or syntactic patterns in corpora;

•             how to determine the internal homogeneity of corpora;

•             how to identify stages in temporally-organized corpora;

•             how to explore differences between different speaker populations with regard to their linguistic behavior.

messages.subject: RNA-Seq, R, and Training
messages.body_plain:
This is prompted by Noam Ross' tweet  <https://twitter.com/noamross/status/456598385709965314>"Was asked about doing RNAseq work in R, which I know nothing about. Is this taught at the BioInf Core trainings?"

There are two overlapping questions here:  1) How is R used in RNA-Seq? 2) Is any R included in UCD Bioinformatics Core Training <http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/>?
To simplify this, the following presumes RNA-Seq with Illumina HiSeq reads.  Typical compressed file sizes are 5-10G (fastq.gz) and ~10G (bam - compressed alignments)

1. R and RNA-Seq
For typical workflow, see slide 3 here <http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/docs/2013/06/rnaseq/_downloads/MB_RNASeq_BC_Aligners_2013.pdf>. Good Bioconductor resources are high-throughput-sequencing <http://bioconductor.org/help/workflows/high-throughput-sequencing/> and RNA-Seq tutorial <http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/html/RnaSeqTutorial.html>. (There are many, many RNA-Seq Bioconductor packages)
Read QC, trimming, and alignment (to reference fasta) are typically done with C programs but there are R packages that perform these functions as well.  (Often, when processing these large files, the R package takes more time and RAM than do most of the equivalent C programs.)
Converting alignments to raw counts per gene can be done in R or with perl/python scripts.  This is a much smaller table.
Statistical analysis of raw counts (normalization, modeling, differential expression, FDR testing, etc.) is typically done in R, but a very common non-R RNA-Seq stats software is cuffdiff <http://cufflinks.cbcb.umd.edu/manual.html#cuffdiff>.
Downstream processing (data visualization, GO Enrichment, Pathway Analysis, etc.) is also commonly done with R packages (edgeR <http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/edgeR.html>, DESeq <http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/DESeq2.html>, cummeRbund <http://compbio.mit.edu/cummeRbund/>, etc.)
(Note: some software, notably Trinity <http://trinityrnaseq.sourceforge.net/analysis/diff_expression_analysis.html>, wraps R packages in perl or python scripts)

2. RNA-Seq Training (UCD Biocore)
(Note: Documentation from past courses is at http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/documentation/)
Our typical trainee is a biologist (grad student/postdoc/researcher/faculty), with little or no exposure to command-line or programming languages. For the last few years we've used the Galaxy GUI platform to concentrate on concepts and workflows rather than the steep command-line learning curve. Although Galaxy is simple for the user, running R in Galaxy is a pain to set up and maintain, requiring XML wrappers to be written to generate the R scripts. So, our 2013 Short Course didn't include any R.  This year, we're teaching two week-long courses -- one in Galaxy <http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/2014/02/13/using-galaxy-for-analysis-of-high-throughput-sequence-data-june-16-20-2014/> and one in command-line <http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/2014/02/13/using-the-linux-command-line-for-analysis-of-high-throughput-sequence-data-september-15-19-2014/>.  Although the topics will be the same, the command-line course might let us try R again.
A few years ago, we experimented with a 2-day Data Visualization in R Workshop, using R Studio, which did cover some RNA-Seq analysis.  It was last taught in 2012 <http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/docs/2012/05/DAV/index.html>, when Vince Buffalo was in our group. I would like to include some of these topics in a more focused RNA-Seq workshop (in late 2014 or 2015).  One challenge we have to teaching R is that most of the bioinformatics core personnel are not statisticians and are also not proficient R programmers. (I mainly "get by" following the vignettes.)

It would be great to get input from you on the incorporation of R into our workshops.  And maybe we could explain some of the challenges and opportunities with RNA-Seq. We could set up a meeting to discuss or come to one of the D-RUG meetings.

Thanks!

Monica Britton

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Replacing entire entries
messages.body_plain:
Elise,

These should be factors, which in R are just integer vectors with some bells and whistles (levels). Rather than matching the strings (which could work), try working with the function levels():

> resp <- factor(sample(c("covered well", "public covered well", "other stuff"), 100, replace=TRUE))
> head(resp)
[1] public covered well other stuff         public covered well
[4] other stuff         public covered well covered well
Levels: covered well other stuff public covered well
> levels(resp)
[1] "covered well"        "other stuff"         "public covered well"
> levels(resp) <- c("well or borehole", "others stuff", "well or borehole")
> head(resp)
[1] well or borehole others stuff     well or borehole others stuff
[5] well or borehole well or borehole
Levels: well or borehole others stuff

The take home points are that (1) levels() returns the factor levels (2) levels() specifies levels *in order* which can be used to merge to levels with levels(resp) <- # your new levels here, with old levels merged.

HTH,
Vince

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I want to time a couple pieces of code to see which is most efficient. I found instructions on line for using proc.time() to do this, but I am getting screwy results.

 time1 = proc.time()
x=5*4*3*2*1
 time2 = proc.time() - time1

 user  system elapsed
  0.004   0.000   0.006

I understood that "elapsed" time should be the sum of "user" and "system" when the code is run as a chunk, but it doesn't seem to work.

Sometimes "user" is significantly more than "elapsed". eg:

   user  system elapsed
 54.681   0.799  30.509

Could this be because I am running things in parallel? If so, what value is of most interest to me in making my code more efficient? Can anyone recommend other ways to time your code?

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Timing my code
messages.body_plain:
Exactly, this is due to using parallel.

User/#cores + system = elapsed

>From ?proc.time:

> The first two entries are the total user and system CPU times of the current
     R process and any child processes on which it has waited, and the
     third entry is the ‘real’ elapsed time since the process was
     started.

For optimization I guess you care about the elapsed time, but if there is significant overhead, you might focus on the user time / #cores.

A more direct way of doing the call in your code snippet would be to use system.time
>system.time(rnorm(1e6))

People like microbenchmark package for timing, but I haven't used it enough to know what to do re timing of child processes.

Hope this helps,
Jaime

messages.body_plain:
Worth noting: Radford Neal has found problems <http://radfordneal.wordpress.com/2014/02/02/inaccurate-results-from-microbenchmark/> with the microbenchmark package.

The short version is that, when comparing two methods, memory operations resulting from one process can consume time that gets assigned to the other one, leading to inaccurate timings.

I'd just use system.time() like Jaime suggested, although Hadley Wickham says it's less precise <http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Performance.html>.  There's also a package called rbenchmark, but I don't know anything about it.

Dave

Can you provide the levels of your two variables and the levels of the combined variable?

And what model formula did you when when you separated the effects in the ANOVA?  (I am wondering if you included an interaction term)

I am guessing that when you created the combination, you effectively created a variable with all combinations of levels. These would be two different models and the appropriate choice will depend on your assumptions and, as Iara noted, also your question.

messages.body_plain:
It is kosher to combine dummy variables, but the coding of the variables can be counter-intuitive. You should get the *same result either way.

Here is an example from a pamphlet I have:
"There are 2 ways to include interaction effects in regression analysis: the two methods calculate and express the interaction effect in slightly different ways.
Method 1: Run separate regressions. If the the z variable has only a few (2 or 3) categories, we can regress y on x separately for each category of the z variable.  This approach has a logic similar to control tables, which are a set of cross-tabulations between an x and y variable separated according to their value on a z variable.
Method 2: Include an interaction term in a single regression equation.  An interaction variable can be created by multiplying two variables together (e.g. compute interact= x * z).  Include the interaction variable and the two independent variables being multiplied together in the regression equation.  These interacting variables can be ordinal, interval, or dummy variables, but for our purposes, we will focus only on dummy z variables.Great care must be taken to ensure that interaction terms are correctly computed. generally, you want to ensure that in multiplying your dummy variables together you obtain a value of 1 only for the category of interest to you. In this case, we expect that being female and over 30 leads to lower income, so we should ensure that our dummy variables Female=1 and over 30=1.
NOTE: using either Method 1 or Method 2 with a dummy z variable and a single x variable provides us with exactly the same information.  The two methods simply express the interaction effect in a slightly different way. "

 More info: http://groups.chass.utoronto.ca/pol242/Labs/interaction07.htm

Sacha

messages.body_plain:
Hi again, Evan,

A model with fish*toads is equivalent to a model with fish + toads + fish:toads.

The ":" operator creates an interaction term equivalent to the product of terms, and does not include the main effects of the individual terms.  On the other hand, the "*" operator creates the interaction and includes the lower order effects.  This means that "fish*toads" will give you the same result as "fish + toads + fish:toads" which will also give you the same result as "fish + toads + fish*toads" (although there is redundancy in this expression).  By including all main effects and interaction (3 model df), then the model is fully specified, and the result is equivalent to a model where you combined the variables into 1 (which is also 3 model df).  Therefore, anova1 and anova2 should be the same, and you should see no differences in their fit (i.e. df, likelihood, residuals, AIC,...etc).

Also, for this reason, then anova2 and anova3 should not be the same.  Whereas anova2 is a full model, anova3 is missing the main effects of fish and toads (i.e. the intercept terms for fish and toads).  In this model, the fish scent has 0 effect in the absence of toads, and the toads have no effect in the absence of fish scent.  Another way to think about this is by taking the mathematical product of fish * toads.  This will give you an indicator variable which is 1 when toads and fish are both present, and 0 when either one of them is absent.  Fit a model (anova5) using this new indicator variable.  This is identical to anova3.  So, anova3 is only useful for comparing tadpole behavior when fish and toads are both present versus tadpole behavior when either one is absent.

anova4 is kind of in-between anova3 and anova1/anova2.  The interaction term in anova4 represents the effect of toads when fish are present.  This model assumes that toads have no effect when fish are absent.

The interaction term in anova1 represents the difference in toad effect on tadpoles when fish are present vs. the toad effect on tadpoles when fish are absent.

It's still unclear to me where you are looking when you say "anova2 gives us a significant result (P < 0.05)."  None of the coefficients for that model directly represents the interaction effect.

I put together this fake analysis based on what you are describing, and what I'm trying to explain.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# a sample of what the data looks like
data = data.frame(list(response=c(5,10,8,2), fish=c(1,1,0,0), toads=c(0,1,1,0), treatment=c("fish","both","toads","neither")))

# here I create fake replicates
moredata = data
for (i in 1:10){
  tmp = data
  tmp$response = data$response + rnorm(4,0,1)
  moredata = rbind(moredata,tmp)
}

# fit 4 versions of the anova
anova1 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fish*toads))
anova2 = with(moredata, aov(response~ treatment))
anova3 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fish:toads))
anova4 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fish + fish:toads))

summary(anova1)
summary(anova2)
summary(anova3)
summary(anova4)

# now fit another anova based on a new indicator based on the product of fish and toads
moredata$fishtoadprod = moredata$fish * moredata$toads
anova5 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fishtoadprod))
summary(anova5)

# compare models (anova3 and anova5 are nested in anova4, so I ordered them hierarchically)
anova(anova1,anova2,anova4,anova3,anova5)
AIC(anova1,anova2,anova4,anova3,anova5)
# note that anova1 is equiv to anova2, and anova3 is equiv to anova5

Glad it helped.  I think that the model.matrix function in R will also help with the understanding.  This displays the design matrix of your formula.  All effects and interactions in a linear model are always expressed as a design matrix in order to fit the model.  I find that whenever there is confusion about what terms are represent in a formula, then it always helps me to look at the design matrix.

model.matrix(anova2)
model.matrix(anova3)
model.matrix(anova4)

> On Wed, Apr 23, 2014 at 8:16 PM, Yee, Julie <juli...@usgs.gov> wrote:
> > Hi again, Evan,
> >
> > A model with fish*toads is equivalent to a model with fish + toads +
> > fish:toads.
> >
> > The ":" operator creates an interaction term equivalent to the product of
> > terms, and does not include the main effects of the individual terms.  On
> > the other hand, the "*" operator creates the interaction and includes the
> > lower order effects.  This means that "fish*toads" will give you the same
> > result as "fish + toads + fish:toads" which will also give you the same
> > result as "fish + toads + fish*toads" (although there is redundancy in this
> > expression).  By including all main effects and interaction (3 model df),
> > then the model is fully specified, and the result is equivalent to a model
> > where you combined the variables into 1 (which is also 3 model df).
> > Therefore, anova1 and anova2 should be the same, and you should see no
> > differences in their fit (i.e. df, likelihood, residuals, AIC,...etc).
> >
> > Also, for this reason, then anova2 and anova3 should not be the same.
> > Whereas anova2 is a full model, anova3 is missing the main effects of fish
> > and toads (i.e. the intercept terms for fish and toads).  In this model, the
> > fish scent has 0 effect in the absence of toads, and the toads have no
> > effect in the absence of fish scent.  Another way to think about this is by
> > taking the mathematical product of fish * toads.  This will give you an
> > indicator variable which is 1 when toads and fish are both present, and 0
> > when either one of them is absent.  Fit a model (anova5) using this new
> > indicator variable.  This is identical to anova3.  So, anova3 is only useful
> > for comparing tadpole behavior when fish and toads are both present versus
> > tadpole behavior when either one is absent.
> >
> > anova4 is kind of in-between anova3 and anova1/anova2.  The interaction term
> > in anova4 represents the effect of toads when fish are present.  This model
> > assumes that toads have no effect when fish are absent.
> >
> > The interaction term in anova1 represents the difference in toad effect on
> > tadpoles when fish are present vs. the toad effect on tadpoles when fish are
> > absent.
> >
> > It's still unclear to me where you are looking when you say "anova2 gives us
> > a significant result (P < 0.05)."  None of the coefficients for that model
> > directly represents the interaction effect.

> > I put together this fake analysis based on what you are describing, and what
> > I'm trying to explain.

> > anova3 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fish:toads))
> > anova4 = with(moredata, aov(response~ fish + fish:toads))
> >

> > summary(anova2)

> >
